final_answer:
The Dead Sea is called "dead" because its extreme salinity—over 34%—makes it nearly impossible for most aquatic life to survive. This high salt concentration is due to a combination of geological and chemical factors. 

Geologically, the Dead Sea lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, a tectonic depression formed by the separation of the Arabian and African plates. Its water has no natural outlet, so evaporation rates are extremely high, leaving behind dissolved minerals. Over millennia, these minerals—primarily magnesium, potassium, calcium, and bromine—have accumulated, creating one of the saltiest bodies of water on Earth.

Chemically, the lack of freshwater inflow means that the only water entering the Dead Sea comes from rivers like the Jordan River and underground springs. As this water evaporates, the salts remain, increasing the salinity. The chemical composition of the surrounding rocks and soil also contributes to the mineral load. The high density of the water (about 1.4 times that of the ocean) further prevents mixing with surrounding waters, reinforcing the isolation of its extreme salinity. 

This combination of geological processes (evaporation, tectonic activity, and mineral deposition) and chemical interactions (salt accumulation and mineral dissolution) explains the Dead Sea’s name and its unique, lifeless environment.
